reading.body:
Government AI activity is now a matter of public record: federal agencies disclose what they run, GAO audits those inventories, and 2,425 state AI bills are tracked to their source.

The pattern is layered oversight. GAO reviews federal AI inventories and management, state legislation is tracked bill by bill, and international indexes from Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, and Stanford HAI compare national readiness, strategies, and policy execution. This makes government AI adoption measurable and auditable, which shapes where and how public-sector systems can operate.

What this record does not show is the physical layer. The Oxford Insights index scores infrastructure as one dimension, but no scores or infrastructure findings appear here. The data covers governance, law, and policy, not the compute, buildings, or power behind the systems being governed.

summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The clearest measured picture of government AI in these sources comes from the U.S. GAO's audit of federal agencies. Twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, described as specific challenges or opportunities AI may solve, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of the reported use cases were in the planning phase and not yet in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported that they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases.

GAO also found the underlying record unreliable and the compliance picture incomplete. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, and two inventories included AI uses that agencies later determined were not AI. Ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing an AI Center of Excellence, while the Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, the Office of Personnel Management had not established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific requirements. GAO notes there is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and that the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI.

On what the technology is actually used for, GAO lists analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, identifying information security threats, and facilitating the review of large datasets. The most visible public-facing deployment described here is America.gov, launched September 29, 2026 by the General Services Administration and the National Design Studio under an executive order, which answers questions in plain language from about 29,000 government websites and runs on Google Gemini and xAI Grok. Phase 1 finds information, and Phase 2, planned for 2027 with Login.gov, is to handle applications and renewals. It offers no public API and its terms bar automated agents, so this site tracks it as a deployment rather than a source. Covered services are public-facing federal services serving more than 100,000 users in a 12-month period that can be accessed or applied for online, with Internal Revenue Service tax filing and national-security-sensitive services excluded.

The regulatory posture is being written mostly at the state level. This site's AI Laws tracker reports 6,030 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database, and its own description of that section cites 2,425 bills. Of 104 measures across 27 states reviewed on September 18, 2026, only Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149 passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors, and every other measure names one setting such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. No state in that set created a new agency to enforce AI law, the attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states simply declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act. New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions under NY S07599, and the recurring rule where stakes are personal is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider.

The international and measurement sources frame the same gap from a distance. Stanford HAI's AI Index describes a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating and adoption spreading while the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate and understand the technology fall behind, in a field where data transparency is declining. OECD.AI, the OECD Artificial Intelligence Policy Observatory, gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives alongside the OECD AI Principles for trustworthy AI that respects human rights and is fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe, and notes that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand. Oxford Insights says it helps governments increase the impact of their public services by empowering teams and harnessing technology, and its Government AI Readiness Index scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure and public-sector adoption.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the practical guidance in this material is to build to the common core of duties that recur across state law: tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits or education, have a crisis protocol and know the age of your user if the product holds a conversation, and keep records of what the system does, because the attorney general is the enforcer you are most likely to meet. Federal agencies face the same discipline problem the private sector does, since GAO found key requirements unmet and no government-wide guidance on acquisition and use. The sources here measure government AI mainly through inventories, audits and legislation rather than through adoption rates, and where they are silent on outcomes and returns, this analysis does not fill the gap.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI describes itself as a policy observatory that helps countries shape trustworthy AI in line with the OECD AI Principles, and says it offers access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog on AI policy. It invites organisations developing advanced AI systems to take part by submitting a report, saying that sharing information would help make risk mitigation measures more transparent and comparable. The observatory states that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI combined under the GPAI brand into one integrated partnership. Its stated purpose is to help AI actors build and use systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe.

https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index.brief: The AI Index, described as an independent programme at Stanford HAI, says its mission is to supply unbiased, rigorously vetted and globally sourced data on artificial intelligence to policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public. This year's edition, the page states, reveals a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with technical capabilities, investment and adoption advancing while the frameworks for governing and evaluating the technology lag and data transparency declines. The programme says previous editions have been cited in newspapers including The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, accumulated hundreds of academic citations, and been referenced by policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It also reports a collaboration with Elif Kiesow Cortez, who founded and leads a law and technology lab at The Hague University of Applied Sciences, on a project using a judicial decision database to improve predictability and legal certainty for AI providers and users. An excerpt from the 2026 report notes "a sharp increase in AI adoption in medicine", including clinical documentation, medical imaging and diagnostic reasoning.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports tracking 6,021 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database and linked to each bill's official page. It says it compared the enrolled text of 104 measures passed across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026, and found that no two states wrote the same law. According to the page, only Colorado (CO SB189) and Texas (TX HB149) passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors, while every other measure names a single setting such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. Where stakes are personal, the page says legislatures repeat the same rule ,  "AI may assist, but it may not be the only decider" ,  citing insurers barred from denying care on an algorithm alone, bans on AI delivering therapy or presenting itself as a licensed clinician, limits on AI as sole course instructor or teacher-evaluation scorer, and a New York requirement for meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. The page states that no state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law, that attorneys general enforce the larger laws often exclusively, that several states treat violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices under consumer protection acts, and that a private right to sue is the exception, appearing mainly where one identifiable person is harmed.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
